# Reference: Communication & information

## Writing (signs that record language) `writing_invention`
- Core idea: Fixed visible signs stand for words of a spoken language, so a message can be read by someone absent or born later. Writing was invented independently at least three times (Mesopotamia, China, Mesoamerica; Egypt possibly a fourth). At Uruk, early tablets combine numerals with signs for goods; early Shang inscriptions record royal divination. One way to extend a script is the rebus principle: a sign for a word is reused for its sound, so names and any sentence can be written ('bee' + 'leaf' for 'belief'). A working system needs a fixed sign list, phonetic use of signs, a cheap durable medium (clay, papyrus, bamboo, bark paper) and people who know its conventions.
- Pitfalls: Thinking writing was invented once and spread: Chinese and Maya writing are independent inventions | Calling any picture or tally 'writing': without a link to the words of a language it records only a few fixed meanings | Assuming early writing was for literature or religion: in Mesopotamia about 85–90 % of the earliest tablets are administrative accounts | Treating the token-to-tablet origin theory (Schmandt-Besserat) as settled fact: it is influential but disputed in detail
- History: mesopotamia: c. 3350–3200 BC – proto-cuneiform accounting tablets at Uruk; by c. 2600 BC cuneiform writes Sumerian sentences and literature; egypt: c. 3250 BC – inscribed labels from tomb U-j at Abydos (dating and independence from Mesopotamia disputed); hieroglyphs fully developed by c. 2700 BC; india: c. 2600–1900 BC – Indus signs on seals, undeciphered; whether they are full writing is disputed; china: c. 1250 BC – Shang oracle-bone inscriptions at Anyang, already a mature script ancestral to modern characters; greece: c. 1450–1400 BC – Linear B, a syllabary for Mycenaean Greek, adapted from Minoan Linear A; americas: c. 300 BC – Maya glyphs at San Bartolo (Guatemala); earlier Olmec and Zapotec signs (Cascajal block c. 900 BC) are disputed
- Read: Peter T. Daniels & William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996) | Andrew Robinson, The Story of Writing (1995) | Denise Schmandt-Besserat, Before Writing (1992)

## Alphabet and mass literacy `alphabet_writing`
- Deps: helped by writing_invention
- Core idea: Use letters to represent the consonants and vowels that distinguish words in a language. A small sign inventory can ease initial instruction. Reading fluently also takes practice, access to texts and teaching. To invent one for a language: say words slowly, list the distinct sounds, give each a simple sign, and teach the sound of each letter (not its name). Greek writers adapted the system by reusing Phoenician signs for consonants they lacked as vowels (aleph to alpha). Korean Hangul (1446) shows a designed alphabet whose basic consonant shapes represent the speech organs.
- Pitfalls: Pressing an alphabet on Chinese: characters bridge mutually unintelligible dialects and distinguish many homophones, so the trade-off is real | Believing the alphabet by itself creates democracy or logic: literacy needs cheap writing material, schools and something to read | Copying another language's spelling: an alphabet only helps if spelling follows the learner's pronunciation | Calling the Phoenician script a full alphabet: it wrote consonants only (an abjad), as Arabic and Hebrew mostly still do
- History: egypt: c. 1900–1800 BC – Semitic-speaking workers adapt hieroglyphs to write their consonants (Wadi el-Hol and Serabit el-Khadim inscriptions); developed in the Levant into the Phoenician 22-letter consonant alphabet by c. 1050 BC; mesopotamia: c. 14th–13th c. BC – Ugarit (Syria) writes a 30-sign alphabet in cuneiform wedges on clay; Aramaic script becomes the administrative script of the Assyrian and Persian empires; greece: c. 800–750 BC – Greeks adopt Phoenician letters and add vowels; rome: 7th c. BC – Latin alphabet from the Etruscan version of the Greek; india: 3rd c. BC – Brahmi script in Ashoka's edicts, an alphasyllabary marking vowels by attached signs (derivation from Aramaic disputed); ancestor of most South and Southeast Asian scripts; islamic: 4th–6th c. – Arabic script develops from Nabataean Aramaic; vowel and dot marks added in the 7th–8th c.; east_asia: 9th c. – Japanese kana syllabaries; 1443 the Korean court records King Sejong's creation of Hangul, promulgated 1446 (Hunminjeongeum); africa: c. 4th c. AD – Ge'ez script adds vowel marks to consonants; c. 1833 Momolu Duwalu Bukele's Vai syllabary in Liberia; americas: 1821 – Sequoyah, himself illiterate, creates the Cherokee syllabary, adopted by most Cherokee within a few years
- Read: Peter T. Daniels & William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996) | Andrew Robinson, The Story of Writing (1995) | Hunminjeongeum (1446)

## Codex book and finding aids `codex_book`
- Deps: helped by paper, alphabet_writing
- Core idea: Fold sheets into gatherings, sew them together along the fold and bind them between boards: the book can be written on both sides, opened at any place, carried and stacked, and lasts. Then add tools for finding: numbered pages or leaves, chapter headings, running heads, a table of contents, spaces between words, punctuation and an alphabetical index giving page numbers. With these a reader can look something up in a minute instead of unrolling a scroll from the start, and read silently and fast.
- Pitfalls: Making an index without fixed page numbers: in hand-copied books pages differ from copy to copy, so indexes refer to chapters; printing made page indexes useful | Assuming the ancients could only read aloud: silent reading is attested in antiquity, the Augustine-and-Ambrose story is over-read | Thinking the codex replaced the scroll because of paper: Roman codices were parchment or papyrus; the change came first among Christians | Forgetting that alphabetical order itself must be taught and agreed before an index works
- History: rome: late 1st c. AD – Martial advertises his poems in pocket parchment codices; 2nd–4th c. Christians prefer the codex; by c. AD 400 codices outnumber rolls; china: bamboo-slip and silk scrolls; 10th–14th c. butterfly and wrapped-back bindings of printed sheets; Ming thread-stitched binding; india: palm-leaf books (pothi) strung on cords through holes, used for two millennia; islamic: 7th–8th c. – parchment codex Qurans; from the 9th c. paper books in Baghdad, with tables of contents and catchwords; americas: Maya and Mexica screenfold books of bark paper coated with lime; the Dresden Codex probably dates from the 11th–13th c.; europe: 7th–8th c. – Irish and Anglo-Saxon scribes separate words; 13th c. alphabetical subject indexes and the Dominican Bible concordance (c. 1230s); 1470 first printed leaf numbers (Cologne)
- Read: Colin H. Roberts & T. C. Skeat, The Birth of the Codex (1983) | Paul Saenger, Space Between Words: The Origins of Silent Reading (1997) | Dennis Duncan, Index, A History of the (2021)

## Woodblock printing `woodblock_printing`
- Deps: helped by paper
- Core idea: Write the page in ink on thin paper, paste it face down on a planed block of fine, even-grained wood (pear, jujube), and carve away the blank wood so the reversed characters stand in relief. Brush on water-based soot ink, lay damp paper on the block and rub its back with a dry brush or pad; no press is needed. One block prints thousands of copies, text and picture are cut together, and blocks are stored for reprints on demand. For a script with thousands of characters it is cheaper than movable type for most print runs. Colour prints use one block per colour, registered by cut corners.
- Pitfalls: Carving the text the right way round: it must be reversed, which pasting the written sheet face down does automatically | Using oily ink for hand-rubbed wood blocks: water-based soot ink with glue works; oil ink is for metal type in a press | Choosing knotty or coarse wood: fine lines break and the block warps | Seeing it as a primitive stage before movable type: in East Asia it remained the main method until the 19th c., by choice | Believing European block books preceded Gutenberg: the surviving ones date from the 1450s onwards
- History: china: 7th–8th c. – printed charms and sutras; 868 the Dunhuang Diamond Sutra, the oldest surviving complete printed book with an explicit date; 932–953 the Confucian classics printed at state expense; 971–983 Kaibao Buddhist canon on some 130,000 blocks; east_asia: by 751 – dharani scroll sealed in the Bulguksa pagoda, Korea (place of printing disputed); 764–770 Japan's Hyakumanto darani, a million printed charms; 1237–1251 Tripitaka Koreana on over 81,000 blocks; islamic: 10th–14th c. – block-printed amulets (tarsh) in Egypt; 1294 notes printed at Tabriz; india: block-printed cotton textiles, exported to Egypt by the 13th c.; book printing only with European presses from 1556; europe: c. 1400 – woodcut devotional images on paper (St Christopher dated 1423); c. 1450s–1470s block books
- Read: Tsien Tsuen-hsuin, Paper and Printing, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 part 1 (1985) | Thomas Francis Carter, The Invention of Printing in China and Its Spread Westward (1925) | Frances Wood & Mark Barnard, The Diamond Sutra: The Story of the World's Earliest Dated Printed Book (2010)

## Movable-type printing press `printing_press`
- Deps: helped by paper, alphabet_writing, woodblock_printing, codex_book
- Core idea: European letterpress combines several techniques. (1) Type: a hardened steel punch is cut for each letter and struck into copper to make a matrix; the matrix sits in an adjustable hand mould into which type metal (lead with tin and antimony) is poured, giving thousands of identical letters of exactly the same height. (2) Ink: lampblack ground in boiled linseed-oil varnish, which clings to metal. (3) Press: a screw press like a wine or paper press presses dampened paper evenly on the inked type. Compositors set letters into lines and pages and redistribute them after printing. A two-man press made roughly 1,500 to 3,000 impressions in a long day.
- Pitfalls: Saying Gutenberg invented printing: woodblock printing is some 600 years older and movable type had been made in China and Korea | Thinking the press was the hard part: the hand mould for casting exact type was the key step | Using water-based ink on metal type (it beads) or pure lead type (too soft, shrinks on cooling): antimony makes the alloy hard and sharp | Underestimating cost and market: paper was the largest expense and many early printers went bankrupt on unsold books | Repeating that the Ottomans banned printing in 1485 as settled fact: the decrees are known only from later European reports and the reasons for slow adoption are debated
- History: china: 1040s – Bi Sheng prints with baked-clay movable type (described by Shen Kuo, Mengxi bitan, 1088); c. 1297–1298 Wang Zhen's wooden type and rotating type tables; c. 1490 Hua Sui prints with bronze type in Wuxi; woodblock remains dominant; east_asia: 1377 – Jikji, printed with metal type at Heungdeok temple, Korea, the oldest surviving metal-type book (earlier Korean metal printing of 1234 is recorded but lost); 1403 royal type foundry; 1590s Japan; europe: c. 1440 – Gutenberg's experiments at Strasbourg; c. 1450 Mainz; 1454–1455 42-line Bible; 1465 Subiaco; 1469 Venice; 1471 Florence; by 1500 presses in some 250 towns; 1514 an Arabic Book of Hours printed with movable type at Fano; islamic: 1493 – Jewish press in Istanbul; 1727 Müteferrika's Ottoman Turkish press; 1822 Bulaq press in Egypt; india: 1556 – Jesuit press at Goa; americas: 1539 – Mexico City (Juan Pablos); 1640 Cambridge, Massachusetts
- Read: Elizabeth L. Eisenstein, The Printing Revolution in Early Modern Europe (1983) | Lucien Febvre & Henri-Jean Martin, L’Apparition du livre (1958; English translation, The Coming of the Book, 1976) | Tsien Tsuen-hsuin, Paper and Printing, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 part 1 (1985)

## Reproducing images (woodcut, engraving, etching, lithography) `lithography_engraving`
- Deps: helped by paper, printing_press, nitric_acid, copper_bronze
- Core idea: Woodcut: lines left in relief on a block, printed with type in the same press. Copper engraving and etching: lines cut with a burin, or bitten by acid through a wax ground scratched with a needle; ink is rubbed into the grooves and wiped off the surface, and a roller press forces damp paper into the lines. It gives far finer detail, for maps and technical drawings. Lithography (1796): draw with a greasy crayon on fine-grained limestone, wet the stone, and greasy ink sticks only to the drawing; no cutting, so any artist can draw directly. Halftone screens (1880s) break photographs into dots that print with type.
- Pitfalls: Trying to print an intaglio plate in the letterpress with the text: it needs a separate roller press and a second pass | Forgetting that every image must be drawn reversed | Expecting copper plates to last indefinitely: they wear after a few thousand impressions unless re-cut or steel-faced | Etching with strong acid in a closed room: the fumes are dangerous | Using any stone for lithography: it needs a fine, even, porous limestone like Solnhofen's
- History: china: 868 – woodcut frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra; 1633 Ten Bamboo Studio colour prints from multiple blocks; east_asia: 1765 – Japanese full-colour woodblock prints (nishiki-e, Harunobu); europe: c. 1430s – copper engraving by goldsmiths in Germany; 1481 Florentine Dante with engravings after Botticelli (Baccio Baldini); c. 1500 etching (Daniel Hopfer); 1796–1798 Senefelder's lithography; 1837 chromolithography (Engelmann); 1882 Meisenbach's halftone; 1904 offset printing
- Read: William M. Ivins Jr., Prints and Visual Communication (1953) | Arthur M. Hind, A History of Engraving and Etching (1923) | Alois Senefelder, A Complete Course of Lithography (1819)

## Relay post and public mail `postal_system`
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing, paved_roads_macadam, paper
- Core idea: Stations a short day's ride apart (some 20–40 km) along fixed roads keep fresh horses or runners; each courier rides one stage and hands on the bag, so a message travels day and night at 150–300 km a day instead of the 30–50 km of a single traveller. Stations log the time each bag arrives, so delays can be traced. The second step is to open the post to everyone at published rates. Rowland Hill's insight (1837): carrying a letter costs little, handling and collecting the fee costs much, so a cheap uniform prepaid rate with an adhesive stamp can raise volume, though revenue may initially fall.
- Pitfalls: Believing the post began with Thurn und Taxis or 1840: Persian, Chinese, Roman, Islamic and Inca relays are far older | Charging by distance and collecting from the recipient: expensive, slow and full of refusals | Forgetting that rulers read the mail: opening letters (black chambers) was routine, so use seals and ciphers | Expecting relay stations to run themselves: they need fodder, pay and inspectors, or they decay | Planning a two-way pigeon post: a pigeon flies only home, so birds must be carried out first
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2100 BC – Ur III royal messengers draw rations at way stations; Neo-Assyrian royal road with relay posts (8th–7th c. BC); c. 500 BC Achaemenid Royal Road from Sardis to Susa with 111 stations (Herodotus 5.52), and the relay riders Herodotus praises (8.98); china: Qin–Han – post stations on main roads, with documents logged by hour (Xuanquan site, 1st c. BC); 13th c. Mongol yam system with over 1,400 stations in China; rome: c. 20 BC – Augustus founds the cursus publicus, a state relay for official mail (Suetonius, Augustus 49); india: 1540s – Sher Shah Suri's mounted post (dak chauki) along the Grand Trunk road; 1854 Indian postage stamps; islamic: 7th–8th c. – Umayyad and Abbasid barid, whose master also reported on governors; 13th c. Mamluk relays and pigeon post between Cairo and Syria; americas: 15th c. – Inca chasqui relay runners on the road network, covering some 200 km a day by report; europe: 1490 – Maximilian I has the Taxis family set up a relay between Innsbruck and Mechelen; 1516 contract for international routes; 1635 English Royal Mail opened to the public; 1840 penny post and Penny Black; 1874 General Postal Union (Bern)
- Read: Herodotus, Histories (c. 430 BC), 5.52–53 and 8.98 | Adam J. Silverstein, Postal Systems in the Pre-Modern Islamic World (2007) | Rowland Hill, Post Office Reform: Its Importance and Practicability (1837)

## Newspapers and periodicals `newspapers_periodicals`
- Deps: helped by printing_press, woodblock_printing, postal_system, free_press
- Core idea: A sheet printed at a regular interval (weekly, later daily) with dated reports from named places, sold by subscription and in the street and later paid for partly by advertisements. Regularity is what makes it work: readers come back, correspondents in many cities send reports by every post, and news becomes a commodity. Name the source and date of each report so readers can judge it. Regular issues depend on gathering and distributing news on time. Handwritten newsletters could circulate to subscribers; printing reached more readers.
- Pitfalls: Calling Rome's Acta diurna or China's court gazettes the first newspapers: they were official bulletins, copied by hand or circulated to officials | Assuming press freedom: licensing, censorship and stamp taxes controlled papers almost everywhere until the 19th c. | Printing unverified rumour: early papers carried many false reports, and printed news spreads panic faster than talk | Expecting profit from sales alone: cheap papers lived from advertising
- History: rome: 59 BC – Caesar has daily public notices (acta diurna) posted, which were copied by hand and sent to the provinces; china: Tang and Song – court gazettes (dibao) circulated to officials, printed by the Song; Ming–Qing Peking Gazette (jingbao) printed and sold by commercial offices; europe: 16th c. – handwritten newsletters (avvisi) from Venice and Rome; 1605 Johann Carolus' Relation in Strasbourg, the first printed weekly; 1650 Leipzig Einkommende Zeitungen, the first daily; 1665 Oxford Gazette, renamed the London Gazette in 1666; 1702 Daily Courant; 1830s penny press; americas: 1690 – Publick Occurrences, Boston, suppressed after one issue; 1704 Boston News-Letter; india: 1780 – Hicky's Bengal Gazette, Calcutta; islamic: 1828 – al-Waqa'i' al-Misriyya, Cairo; 1831 Takvim-i Vekayi, Istanbul; east_asia: 1871 – Yokohama Mainichi, Japan's first Japanese-language daily; 1883 Hanseong sunbo in Korea
- Read: Andrew Pettegree, The Invention of News: How the World Came to Know About Itself (2014) | Johannes Weber, Strassburg, 1605: The Origins of the Newspaper in Europe, German History 24 (2006)

## Scientific journal and peer review `scientific_journal`
- Deps: needs printing_press; helped by postal_system, scientific_academy, reproducibility_open_publication
- Core idea: A periodical that prints short reports of new observations and experiments, dated and with enough detail of method that others can repeat them. Priority goes to whoever publishes first, so discoverers publish instead of keeping secrets, and readers can test and criticise. An editor gathers reports through correspondence; later, referees judge submissions before printing. Minimum: a regular schedule, an editor, a correspondence network, method and measurement in each report, and openness to authors who are not members.
- Pitfalls: Thinking peer review began in 1665: the Royal Society's Committee of Papers selected articles from 1752; its archive of specialist referees’ reports begins in the 1830s | Believing publication proves a result true: it only makes it open to being checked | Publishing results without method and measurements: nobody can repeat them | Expecting craftsmen to share trade secrets: they need priority or patent protection first
- History: islamic: c. 997 – al-Biruni and Ibn Sina exchange written questions and answers on physics, an example of open scholarly controversy, but no periodical; europe: 5 January 1665 – Journal des sçavans, Paris; 6 March 1665 Philosophical Transactions, edited by Henry Oldenburg; 1682 Acta Eruditorum, Leipzig; 1752 Royal Society Committee of Papers; 1869 Nature; americas: 1818 – American Journal of Science; 1880 Science
- Read: Aileen Fyfe, Noah Moxham, Julie McDougall-Waters & Camilla Mørk Røstvik, A History of Scientific Journals: Publishing at the Royal Society, 1665–2015 (2022) | David A. Kronick, A History of Scientific and Technical Periodicals (1962)

## Encyclopedias and dictionaries `encyclopedia_reference_works`
- Deps: helped by printing_press, alphabet_writing, lithography_engraving, codex_book
- Core idea: Collect what is known into one work, ordered alphabetically or by subject, with cross-references and an index, so that anyone can look up a fact or a technique without a teacher. The Encyclopédie added detailed plates of the crafts, making trade knowledge public. A dictionary does the same for words: it fixes spelling and meaning, which a printed national literature needs. Method: a plan of headings, many contributors each writing on what they know, an editor who checks and cross-refers, and subscription to finance a long work.
- Pitfalls: Compiling from books without checking: Pliny and the medieval encyclopedias repeated monsters and errors for centuries | Underestimating scale: the Encyclopédie took 21 years, 28 volumes and some 150 contributors and was banned in between | Assuming it is a European idea: Chinese leishu and Arabic encyclopedias are far older and larger | Forgetting that reference works age: they need new editions
- History: rome: AD 77–79 – Pliny the Elder's Natural History in 37 books; china: c. AD 100 – Xu Shen's Shuowen jiezi, a dictionary of 9,353 characters by radicals; 220s first leishu (classified encyclopedia); 977–983 Taiping yulan in 1,000 chapters; 1403–1408 Yongle dadian, some 11,000 volumes, mostly lost; 1782 Siku quanshu; india: c. 4th–6th c. – Amarakosha, a Sanskrit thesaurus; islamic: c. 977 – al-Khwarizmi's Mafatih al-'ulum (Keys of the Sciences); 10th c. Epistles of the Brethren of Purity; 14th c. al-Nuwayri's Nihayat al-arab; 1412 al-Qalqashandi; europe: c. 630 – Isidore of Seville's Etymologies; c. 1250 Vincent of Beauvais; 1612 Vocabolario degli Accademici della Crusca (Florence); 1728 Chambers' Cyclopaedia; 1751–1772 Diderot and d'Alembert's Encyclopédie; 1755 Johnson's Dictionary; 1768–1771 Encyclopaedia Britannica
- Read: Denis Diderot & Jean le Rond d'Alembert (eds.), Encyclopédie (1751–1772) | Robert Darnton, The Business of Enlightenment: A Publishing History of the Encyclopédie (1979) | Ann Blair, Too Much to Know: Managing Scholarly Information before the Modern Age (2010)

## Library catalogue and classification `library_catalogue`
- Deps: helped by codex_book, alphabet_writing
- Core idea: Every item gets a shelf mark; a catalogue lists each by author, title and subject with its mark, so anything can be found without the librarian's memory. Write each entry on a separate slip or card kept in a drawer: new entries slot in alphabetically and the catalogue never needs rewriting. A classification groups books by subject with numbers that can be subdivided (Dewey: ten main classes, decimal subdivisions), and shelving by relative position lets collections grow. Add a lending register and copies of what is rare.
- Pitfalls: Keeping the catalogue in a bound book: it fills up and cannot stay in order | Fixing books to numbered shelves: every new acquisition breaks the order | Ignoring fire, damp and insects: most ancient libraries were lost slowly, and the single great burning of Alexandria is legend | Lending without a record: books vanish
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2000–1800 BC – Nippur tablets list titles of literary works; 7th c. BC Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh with colophons naming owner and series; greece: 3rd c. BC – Callimachus' Pinakes at Alexandria, 120 books listing authors by subject with works and first lines; china: c. 6 BC – Liu Xiang and Liu Xin catalogue the Han imperial library (Qilüe); from the 7th c. the four-part classification (classics, histories, masters, collections); islamic: 987–988 – Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist, a catalogue of all books in Arabic known to him; large endowed libraries in Baghdad, Cairo and Córdoba; europe: 1545 – Conrad Gessner's Bibliotheca universalis; 1791 French revolutionary inventory written on playing cards, an early card catalogue; americas: 1876 – Dewey Decimal Classification; 1901 Library of Congress sells printed catalogue cards
- Read: Lionel Casson, Libraries in the Ancient World (2001) | Andrew Pettegree & Arthur der Weduwen, The Library: A Fragile History (2021) | Melvil Dewey, A Classification and Subject Index for Cataloguing and Arranging the Books and Pamphlets of a Library (1876)

## Pencil, steel pen and durable ink `pencil_steel_pen`
- Deps: helped by paper
- Core idea: Pencil: powdered graphite mixed with clay, pressed into rods and fired, then glued into a grooved wood casing; more clay gives a harder, paler lead (Conté 1795), so good pencils do not need pure graphite. Steel nib: pressed from thin sheet steel, slit, hardened and tempered; it lasts for weeks where a quill needs recutting every few pages. Fountain pen: a reservoir feeds ink through a channel that also admits air, so flow is steady. Iron-gall ink (crushed oak galls, iron sulphate and gum arabic) is cheap and permanent but acidic.
- Pitfalls: Thinking pencils contain lead: they contain graphite, mistaken for a lead ore ('plumbago') | Using iron-gall ink with steel nibs or too much vitriol: it corrodes the nib and eats the paper over decades | A fountain pen without an air path blots or stops | Assuming the ballpoint is old: it became practical only with Bíró's 1938 design
- History: egypt: c. 3000 BC – reed pens and carbon ink on papyrus; china: by Han – hair brushes and moulded soot-and-glue ink sticks; islamic: 953 – a pen with its own ink reservoir is made for the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz (account by al-Qadi al-Nu'man; design details unknown); europe: late antiquity onwards – iron-gall ink; 16th c. Borrowdale graphite used for marking, 1565 Gessner describes a wooden-cased pencil; 1795 Conté's fired graphite-clay leads; 1820s–1830s Birmingham mass-produces steel nibs; 1884 Waterman's fountain pen; 1938 Bíró's ballpoint patent
- Read: Henry Petroski, The Pencil: A History of Design and Circumstance (1990)

## Shorthand (stenography) `shorthand`
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing
- Core idea: A script of very simple strokes, one per sound, with vowels left out or shown by position and fixed signs for the commonest words, so a trained writer keeps up with speech (over 100 words a minute). With it, debates, trials, sermons and lectures can be recorded word for word and checked later. It must be a fixed published system that others can read, and transcribed into ordinary writing soon after.
- Pitfalls: Inventing personal abbreviations: nobody else, and soon not even the writer, can read them | Basing it on spelling rather than sound: English spelling makes that slow | Expecting quick results: it takes months of daily practice
- History: greece: 4th c. BC – an inscription from the Athenian Acropolis describes a shorthand system; rome: 63 BC – Plutarch says that Cicero stationed trained shorthand writers to record Cato’s Senate speech; the later shorthand tradition names Cicero’s freedman Tiro; europe: 1588 – Timothy Bright's Characterie; 1660s Pepys keeps his diary in Shelton's shorthand; 1834 Gabelsberger (German); 1837 Isaac Pitman's phonetic system; 1888 Gregg publishes Light-Line Phonography in Liverpool; americas: 1890s – Gregg promotes his shorthand in the United States
- Read: Plutarch, Cato the Younger 23 (c. AD 100) | Isaac Pitman, Stenographic Sound-Hand (1837)

## Typewriter `typewriter`
- Deps: helped by interchangeable_parts, precision_measurement, alphabet_writing
- Core idea: Each key works a lever that swings a type slug against an inked ribbon onto paper held on a rubber roller (platen); an escapement moves the carriage one letter width after each stroke, a lever turns the roller one line, and a shift moves the type so each slug carries two characters. It writes uniform, legible text faster than a pen and makes several copies at once with carbon paper. It needs many small precise steel parts and springs, so it became practical only with mass production.
- Pitfalls: Building it before cheap precision parts exist: dozens of earlier designs were single, hand-made curiosities | Repeating that QWERTY was designed to slow typists: the layout evolved over several designs; the precise role of type-bar jams is disputed | Assuming it cannot work for Chinese: Chinese typewriters with trays of some 2,500 characters were made from the 1910s
- History: europe: 1714 – Henry Mill's English patent (no machine known); 1808 Pellegrino Turri builds a machine for a blind countess; 1865–1870 Malling-Hansen's writing ball in Denmark, sold commercially; americas: 1868 – Sholes, Glidden and Soule patent; 1874 Remington No. 1; 1878 shift key (Remington No. 2); east_asia: 1915 – Sugimoto Kyōta's Japanese typewriter; china: 1916 – Zhou Houkun's Chinese typewriter; 1920s Commercial Press models
- Read: Richard N. Current, The Typewriter and the Men Who Made It (1954) | Thomas S. Mullaney, The Chinese Typewriter: A History (2017)

## Copying documents (copying press, carbon paper, stencil duplicator) `copying_duplicating`
- Deps: helped by paper, typewriter, printing_press
- Core idea: Ways to duplicate a document without recopying it by hand. Copying press (Watt 1780): write in a slow-drying gummed ink, press the letter against a damp sheet of thin tissue, and read the mirror copy through the back. Carbon paper: a thin sheet coated with pigment in wax, placed between sheets, gives copies under the pressure of a stylus or typewriter. Stencil duplicator: a waxed sheet is cut by a stylus or a typewriter without ribbon, and ink is forced through the cuts onto paper, giving hundreds of copies. Any office, club or society can then issue circulars, reports and pamphlets without a printer.
- Pitfalls: Ordinary ink in a copying press does not transfer: special copying ink is needed | Expecting carbon or spirit copies to last: many fade | Forgetting the political effect: easy copying escapes censorship and licensing of printers
- History: europe: 1780 – James Watt patents the letter-copying press; 1806 Ralph Wedgwood's carbon paper; 1870s gelatin hectograph; 1881 Gestetner's cyclostyle stencil; americas: 1876 – Edison's electric pen for stencils; 1887 A. B. Dick's mimeograph; 1938 Chester Carlson's xerography, commercial office copier 1959
- Read: JoAnne Yates, Control through Communication: The Rise of System in American Management (1989)

## Braille (tactile writing for blind people) `braille_tactile_writing`
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing, printing_press
- Core idea: Each letter is a pattern of up to six raised dots in a cell two dots wide and three high, read with the fingertip, which feels dots far better than embossed letter shapes. It is written with a stylus and slate, pressing dots from the back, so the writer works right to left. A school that brings blind children together is the place where it spreads.
- Pitfalls: Embossing ordinary Roman letters for the blind (Haüy): hard to read and impossible to write by hand | Equating blindness with lack of intelligence | Calling Barbier’s raised-dot system a military code: his publications propose tactile writing for blind readers; Braille’s smaller six-dot cell was easier to read
- History: europe: 1784 – Haüy's school for the blind; 1829 Louis Braille publishes his system, officially adopted in France 1854; east_asia: 1890 – Ishikawa Kuraji's Japanese braille
- Read: Louis Braille, Procédé pour écrire les paroles, la musique et le plain-chant au moyen de points (1829) | Philippa Campsie, Charles Barbier: A Hidden Story (2021)

## Sign languages of deaf people `sign_languages`
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing
- Core idea: Sign languages of deaf communities are full languages with their own grammar, not mime; teaching deaf children in sign plus writing gives them language and schooling, and a manual alphabet spells names. A school that brings deaf children together is the place where a sign language spreads.
- Pitfalls: Forcing deaf children to lip-read and speak only (oralism after the 1880 Milan congress): many end up with no full language | Believing sign language is universal or simply gestured spoken language: each community has its own | Equating deafness with lack of intelligence
- History: greece: c. 360 BC – Plato's Cratylus mentions deaf people communicating by signs; islamic: 15th–17th c. – deaf attendants (dilsiz) at the Ottoman court use a sign language, learned by courtiers; europe: 16th c. – Pedro Ponce de León teaches deaf children of nobles in Spain; 1620 Juan Pablo Bonet's manual alphabet; 1760 Abbé de l'Épée's school for the deaf, Paris; americas: 1817 – American School for the Deaf, Hartford (Gallaudet and Clerc); Plains Indian Sign Language used between nations
- Read: Harlan Lane, When the Mind Hears: A History of the Deaf (1984) | Oliver Sacks, Seeing Voices (1989)

## Knowledge in the vernacular; translation movements `vernacular_translation`
- Deps: helped by printing_press, alphabet_writing, universal_schooling
- Core idea: Write learned and practical knowledge (medicine, law, mathematics, technique, scripture) in the language people speak, and translate key works into it. Anyone who can read their mother tongue can then learn, check and argue, instead of only those trained in Latin, classical Chinese or Sanskrit. Large organised translation programmes, with patrons paying teams of bilingual scholars to render whole libraries, move a civilisation's knowledge into another. Technical terms must be coined and kept consistent, and one dialect chosen as the written standard.
- Pitfalls: Ignoring the danger: translating scripture could be heresy (Tyndale was executed in 1536) | Forgetting what the learned language gave: an audience across all of Europe or East Asia; scholars kept writing Latin for that reason | Translating without fixed technical terms: every translator invents his own and the texts cannot be compared | Assuming translation began with the Renaissance: the Arabic translation movement and Chinese Buddhist translations are earlier and larger
- History: china: 2nd–7th c. – Buddhist scriptures translated from Indian languages in large state-sponsored bureaus (Kumarajiva c. 400, Xuanzang 7th c.); 1917 movement for writing in vernacular Chinese (baihua); india: 5th c. BC onwards – the Buddha teaches in vernacular Prakrit rather than Sanskrit; 12th–17th c. devotional poets write in regional languages (Tulsidas' Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, 1570s); islamic: 8th–10th c. – the Graeco-Arabic translation movement in Baghdad renders Greek, Syriac, Persian and Sanskrit science and philosophy into Arabic (Hunayn ibn Ishaq); east_asia: 1446 – Hangul promulgated so that common people can write; Korean translations of Buddhist and Confucian texts follow; europe: 12th c. – Toledo translations from Arabic into Latin; c. 1304 Dante defends the vernacular; 1380s Wycliffite Bible; 1522–1534 Luther's German Bible; 1632 Galileo's Dialogue in Italian; 1637 Descartes' Discourse in French
- Read: Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998) | Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (2006) | Peter Burke, Languages and Communities in Early Modern Europe (2004)

## Beacons, flag codes and heliograph `signal_beacons_flag_codes`
- Deps: helped by glass_mirrors, telescope
- Core idea: Visual signals over long distances: fire by night, smoke by day, flags or mirrors. A chain of beacons on hilltops passes a single agreed message ('the enemy is coming') hundreds of kilometres in an hour. To send any message you need a code: Polybius' torch code lays the alphabet in a 5 x 5 grid and shows the row and column by numbers of torches; naval codes give each flag a digit and each number a word or sentence in a codebook (Popham, 1800). The heliograph flashes sunlight from a mirror in Morse code over 50 km or more.
- Pitfalls: A beacon chain sends only what was agreed in advance; a false alarm cannot be called back | Spelling out messages letter by letter: use a codebook of words and phrases | Forgetting that the enemy can see and read the signals | Weather and night stop flags and heliographs
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1780 BC – letters from Mari report fire signals between towns; greece: 458 BC – Aeschylus' Agamemnon describes a beacon chain from Troy (literary); c. 350 BC Aeneas Tacticus' synchronised water-vessel signal; 2nd c. BC Polybius (Histories X.43–47) describes his torch alphabet; china: Han – frontier beacon towers (fengsui) with written rules on the number of fires and smokes for each kind of incursion (Juyan documents); rome: signal towers along frontiers and coasts; europe: 1588 – English beacon chain warns of the Armada; 1800 Popham's numerical flag code; 1857 British Commercial Code of Signals, later the International Code of Signals; 1869 Mance's heliograph; americas: 1860 – Myer's wig-wag flag signalling for the US Army; Plains peoples' smoke signals; india: 1870s – heliographs used on the North-West Frontier and in Afghanistan
- Read: Polybius, Histories X.43–47 (2nd c. BC) | Gerard J. Holzmann & Björn Pehrson, The Early History of Data Networks (1995)

## Optical telegraph (semaphore network) `optical_telegraph`
- Deps: helped by telescope, signal_beacons_flag_codes
- Core idea: A chain of towers on high points 10–15 km apart, each with a mechanism of movable arms (Chappe: a crossbar with two arms set by ropes and pulleys) or shutters (Murray, Edelcrantz). An operator reads the next tower through a telescope and repeats each sign. A codebook turns pairs of signs into numbered words and phrases, so few signs make a sentence. On the Paris–Lille line a single sign could travel some 200 km in minutes. A dispatch took longer: the operators had to relay a succession of signs, and poor visibility could interrupt transmission. Add rules for repeating back and correcting errors.
- Pitfalls: Placing towers too far apart or hidden by haze: reliable distance is about 10–15 km even with telescopes | Sending letter by letter instead of with a phrase codebook | Forgetting that night, fog and rain stop the line | Assuming privacy: operators and watchers can read the signs, so use codes; France made it a state monopoly (1837)
- History: europe: 1684 – Robert Hooke proposes a signalling system to the Royal Society; 1792 Chappe's demonstration; 1794 Paris–Lille line reports the recapture of Condé; 1794–1796 Edelcrantz in Sweden and Murray's shutter line London–Deal; 1832 Prussian line Berlin–Koblenz; by the 1840s France has over 500 stations; replaced by the electric telegraph from the 1850s
- Read: Gerard J. Holzmann & Björn Pehrson, The Early History of Data Networks (1995) | Ignace Chappe, Histoire de la télégraphie (1824)

## Standard time and time zones `standard_time_zones`
- Deps: needs mechanical_clock; helped by electric_telegraph, railway, longitude_chronometer
- Core idea: Local solar time changes by 4 minutes for every degree of longitude, so each town keeps a different noon. That is harmless until railways need timetables and telegraphs need simultaneous times. Solution: one standard time per zone, normally 15 degrees wide (one hour), with offsets usually in whole hours from Greenwich (some use half or quarter hours), and time signals sent by telegraph (or a time ball dropped at a fixed hour) to set all clocks. Local life can keep its noon; trains, telegraphs and courts use zone time.
- Pitfalls: Drawing zones exactly on meridians: borders and trade areas matter more | Confusing zone time with daylight saving time | Expecting acceptance: cities kept local time for decades (Bombay until 1955); France used Paris time until 1911 | Forgetting that prayer times and markets may still follow the sun (Ottoman 'alaturka' time counted from sunset until 1925)
- History: europe: 1840 – Great Western Railway runs on London time; 1847 Railway Clearing House adopts Greenwich time; 1852 Greenwich time signals by telegraph; 1880 Greenwich Mean Time made legal in Britain; americas: 18 November 1883 – US and Canadian railways adopt five zones, including Intercolonial time in eastern Canada; 1884 International Meridian Conference chooses Greenwich; 1918 Standard Time Act; east_asia: 1888 – Japan Standard Time at 135° E; india: 1906 – Indian Standard Time at 82.5° E; Calcutta and Bombay keep local time for decades; china: 1912 – five zones proposed, adopted in 1939; from 1949 one Beijing time for the whole country; islamic: 1925 – Turkey replaces sunset-based time with zone time
- Read: Ian R. Bartky, Selling the True Time: Nineteenth-Century Timekeeping in America (2000) | Vanessa Ogle, The Global Transformation of Time, 1870–1950 (2015)
